newsitem.title: USA: Calif. quake agency to begin operations Dec. 2 - CEO.
newsitem.headline: Calif. quake agency to begin operations Dec. 2 - CEO.

text.p: The California Earthquake Authority (CEA) begins operations on December 2, the authority's interim chief executive officer said Tuesday.
Interim CEO Greg Butler said state Insurance Commissioner Chuck Quackenbush would issue the official certification order for the authority later on Tuesday.
Butler said the authority secured the backing of 71.6 percent of California's residential insurance market, just over the 70 percent required.
"We are on target to begin operations on Monday," Butler told a meeting of the CEA's governing board in Sacramento.
Butler told Reuters after the meeting that the California Earthquake Authority's operations should boost the state's sluggish real estate market.
"The first quarter of 1997 should be very good for the homeowners market," Butler said.
Butler expected the CEA to issue less than 10,000 earthquake policies in its first month of operations.
On Monday, Butler said the authority had secured the backing of 69.7 percent of California's residential insurance market, just short of the 70 percent that was required.
Butler announced on Tuesday that CNA Financial Corp's CNA Insurance, which represents nearly one percent of the market, had agreed to participate.

He said the authority's governing board also voted on Tuesday to incorporate the state's independent Fair Access to Insurance Requirement (FAIR) plan within the CEA, bringing the participation level to 71.6 percent.
The FAIR plan provides homeowners insurance to those that cannot find insurance elsewhere.
Insurance companies representing at least 70 percent of the California residential insurance market had to agree to participate in the earthquake authority for the authority to become operational.

With the participation of 70 percent of the market, the insurance industry would contribute an initial $700 million to fund the earthquake authority. The industry would be obligated to make additional capital commitments to pay claims if an earthquake strikes.
